newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish budget proposal inflation-neutral - c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Finnish budget proposal inflation-neutral - c.bank.

text.p: A more austere 1998 Finnish budget -- which the finance ministry has said aims to prevent the need for monetary tightening -- is neutral on inflation, Bank of Finland board member Matti Vanhala said on Wednesday.

The government is due on August 13 to start a final round of talks on the budget, after the finance ministry proposed deeper cuts to put the deficit at 17 billion markka instead of 21 billion as earlier planned.
Vanhala said the 1998 state budget proposal was a "welcome and important" plan to cut spending more with strong growth.
"At least according to our analysis, the impact on inflation is really pretty neutral," he told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) in an interview due for broadcast later on Wednesday.
"Of course, this kind of economic growth will not go on forever, and it would be better to use this time to consolidate (state finances) further," Vanhala said.
Finland's economic growth is forecast between four and five percent this year and around 3.5 percent next year.
Vanhala said the outlook for inflation was "very much the same as it was in June," when the bank warned that inflation pressures may emerge and cause monetary tightening.

"We are of course conscious of the risk of inflation with the kind of growth rates that we have but a careful look at the indicators and all the available evidence, including anecdotal evidence, suggest that an actual emergence of inflation pressures is not really evident," Vanhala said.
"Monetary policy remains geared to the inflation target so that if, fiscal policy or not, if there is an emergence of inflation pressures, we will of course react with monetary policy," he said.
Vanhala said the next round of collective wage talks late this year would be a key factor for the inflation outlook, but declined to say what level of pay hikes would be considered moderate.

On foreign exchange rates, Vanhala said he assumed that the ERM central parity rate would be a fair and likely conversion rate for the markka into the new euro if Finland joins Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Vanhala said that although the Bundesbank's policy was important for the Bank of Finland, there could not be a common monetary policy as long as the composition of EMU had not been decided.
But exchange rates were a constraint to be considered:

"I think it is fair enough to say that to some extent... the ambition to have a stable exchange rate is a kind of constraint to be kept in mind, but we have said that monetary stability in a broader sense (low inflation) is our primary objective."
"So far there has been no real conflict between these targets," he added.
